# the divide & conquer dominator as a call tree
#
# Regenerate with:  python -m tools.make_traces
# Do not edit by hand: tests/test_docs_traces.py compares this file with a
# fresh run of the code it shows.

## divide_and_conquer([3, 1, 3, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3])

Each node shows its range and the answer it returned; '-' means 'this range
has no dominator'.  Follow the right half: 3 dominates [4..7] because it is
the candidate of both its halves.

`-- majority(lo=0, hi=7)  -> 3
    |-- majority(lo=0, hi=3)  -> '-'
    |   |-- majority(lo=0, hi=1)  -> '-'
    |   |   |-- majority(lo=0, hi=0)  -> 3
    |   |   `-- majority(lo=1, hi=1)  -> 1
    |   `-- majority(lo=2, hi=3)  -> '-'
    |       |-- majority(lo=2, hi=2)  -> 3
    |       `-- majority(lo=3, hi=3)  -> 2
    `-- majority(lo=4, hi=7)  -> 3
        |-- majority(lo=4, hi=5)  -> '-'
        |   |-- majority(lo=4, hi=4)  -> 3
        |   `-- majority(lo=5, hi=5)  -> 4
        `-- majority(lo=6, hi=7)  -> 3
            |-- majority(lo=6, hi=6)  -> 3
            `-- majority(lo=7, hi=7)  -> 3

## the same recursion on [3, 1, 3, 2] -- where it returns nothing

No half has a dominator, so no range above them can have one either.  That
is the halving lemma doing the work: it is what makes 'nothing' a safe
answer to propagate upwards.

`-- majority(lo=0, hi=3)  -> '-'
    |-- majority(lo=0, hi=1)  -> '-'
    |   |-- majority(lo=0, hi=0)  -> 3
    |   `-- majority(lo=1, hi=1)  -> 1
    `-- majority(lo=2, hi=3)  -> '-'
        |-- majority(lo=2, hi=2)  -> 3
        `-- majority(lo=3, hi=3)  -> 2
